title: Rabbi Abba of Akko
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: He was the head in the town of Akko, which stands on the northern border of the Land of Israel on the seashore; and Rabbi Abba, when he went up from Babylonia to the Land of Israel (for Babylonia lies to the north of the Land of Israel, as in Bava Batra 25b and Gittin 6a; Tosafot on Shabbat 65b disagree with Rashi, and in Bekhorot 55b Tosafot wrote that it is to the northeast; Seder HaDorot cites from Yuchasin “Rabbi Abba of Ammo, as in chapter Makom SheNahagu,” and Seder HaDorot wonders at this, and the plain sense is that there, 51a, it is explicit that Akko is outside the Land) — when he came to Akko, as related in Avodah Zarah 34b: a ship of fish-brine that came to the harbor of Akko — Rabbi Abba of Akko set guards with it; Rabbi Abba (Hyman considers “Rava” a scribal error, or an abbreviation for Rabbi Ba) said to him: “Until now, who guarded it?” And in Ketubot 22a: “Rabbi Zeira said: This matter I heard from Rabbi Abba, and were it not for Rabbi Abba of Akko I would have forgotten it.”

Hyman suggests that since the town of Akko was on the border, Rabbi Abba left his place and moved his residence to Caesarea, the place of Rabbi Abbahu, who was close to the government and protected Israel with all his might from the great decrees that arose after Rabbi Yochanan’s death; Rabbi Abba founded a great study house there. He was also poor and greatly in debt, as in Sotah 40a, where Rabbi Abbahu said: “At first I said I am humble; once I saw Rabbi Abba of Akko, who gives one reason and his public interpreter gives another reason, and he does not mind, I said I am not humble.” When the Rabbis wanted to appoint Rabbi Abbahu as head (after Rabbi Ami’s death), once he saw that Rabbi Abba of Akko had many creditors, he said to them: “There is a great man.”

But Hyman finds no report of his appointment as head; he likewise finds no name for the head of the academy after Rabbi Ami’s death in the Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon. Of the teaching of Rabbi Abba of Akko Hyman finds nothing except one aggadic saying that remained to us as a remnant, in Bereshit Rabbah 15:7 and Pesikta deRav Kahana, historical locator 142., where he said: “The tree from which the first Adam ate was a citron.”

notes.text: Restore with ALL his might from supplied כחו; והנין בבל כחו is read והגין בכל כחו. Keep Ammo in the quoted Yuchasin form but Akko in the contextual Sotah reference. אמורא is the public interpreter. Saved Davidson AZ34b retains Rava where Hyman proposes Abba or RabbiBa; no blanket correction. Hyman’s migration, political account, one-surviving-saying claim and academy vacancy remain his statements. Historical Pesikta142. is preserved without page/column equivalence proof.

The consulted Avodah Zarah 34b retains Rava in the Akko brine-ship account, beside Hyman’s Abba/Ba proposal. All his might remains in the body. Ammo in the Yuchasin quotation and Akko in the contextual account remain separate readings. Migration, political protection, academy vacancy and only-surviving-saying claims stay Hyman-attributed; historical Pesikta 142. has no admitted modern page equivalence.
